content: The patient monitoring systems assessment checklist, adapted from an unpublished document, is a tool designed to evaluate the presence and quality of key components in patient monitoring systems. This assessment should be tailored to the specific healthcare setting and conducted at the start of each annual patient monitoring review visit. The checklist evaluates the integration of systems and national tools, human resource capacity, efficiency of patient and data flow, and the accuracy and completeness of data collection, transfer, and reporting. Each sub-checklist includes a list of recommended actions for immediate implementation by the review team. Following the assessment, the review team should outline a follow-up plan, detailing actions required at the national level or during subsequent site visits. The final overall assessment determines whether the facility is capable of completing the remainder of the Annual Patient Monitoring Review (APMR). The checklist includes a series of questions to determine whether the necessary patient monitoring elements are in place. For each statement, the health center should indicate Yes, No, or Not Applicable (N/A). Any No responses indicate areas that require improvement or implementation. Integrated Systems 1. Are the patient monitoring systems for HIV, MNCH/HIV, and TB/HIV integrated? For antenatal care (ANC) and prevention of mother-to-child transmission (PMTCT), are HIV patient monitoring tools used in the MNCH setting? List all tools. Are TB patient monitoring tools used in the MNCH setting? List all tools. Do MNCH patient monitoring tools include HIV elements, such as maternal health cards, ANC registers, labor records, and child health cards? Is there a separate patient record for HIV-exposed infants? Is there an HIV-exposed infant or mother–infant pair register, and is it linked to the ANC or ART register entries for the mother? Are HIV patient monitoring tools used in the TB clinic? List all tools. Integration may also include other programs, such as hepatitis or non-communicable diseases (e.g., hypertension, diabetes). Adapt as appropriate. Human Resources 1. Have all relevant staff in HIV clinics received training on the national patient monitoring system within the past specified months? This includes doctors, nurses, data clerks, lay counselors, and other staff. Specify the number of staff trained and the tools they are trained to use (e.g., cards, registers, reports, data use). Are HIV staff trained in the use of TB patient monitoring tools? If any staff are not trained, the district team should schedule and provide appropriate training or retraining, followed by hands-on support within 2–4 weeks. Availability of Tools 1. Are the following national patient monitoring tools available in adequate supply? Patient-held cards, HIV patient cards, community ART monitoring tools, ART registers, cross-sectional reports, ART cohort analysis reports, appointment books, and transfer/referral forms. Use of Tools 1. Is the facility using the national patient monitoring tools? If additional or alternative tools are being used, list them and explain the reasons for their use. If the facility is using non-standard tools due to gaps in the national system, this should be reported to the Ministry of Health (MoH) for follow-up. Organization and Storage 1. Are HIV patient cards and ART registers well-organized and stored securely? If records are not well-organized, identify the reasons (e.g., lack of space, storage structure, or systematic organization). Patient and Data Flow 1. Is patient and data flow well-defined and efficient? HIV patient cards should be pulled from storage for all patients at the start of the day, follow patients through care, and be returned to registration after each visit. If data flow is inefficient, discuss with the facility team to understand the gaps and use flow diagrams if necessary. Data Completeness and Accuracy 1. Take a sample of five HIV patient cards and check for completeness and accuracy. Verify that encounter pages are filled for each visit, including TB status, weight, pregnancy status, and nutritional assessments for infants. ART Registers 1. ART registers should be filled in following ART initiation and updated with each patient visit. Reporting 1. Cross-sectional and ART cohort reports should be completed and submitted on time. If reports are incomplete or inaccurate, work with health workers to review and address gaps. Appointment and Referral Systems 1. A functioning appointment system should be in place to log patient visits, prepare for clinic days, and follow up on missed appointments. Standard transfer forms should be used to transfer and receive patients, ensuring continuity of care. Data Use 1. Health workers should regularly review patient charts and use collected data to inform patient care and program monitoring. Data use should be a routine part of quality care and treatment, supported by regular site visits from the district management team. Final Action Plan 1. Do not proceed with the APMR if critical elements, such as the HIV patient card or ART registers, are not being used at all. If these tools are in place but require improvement, proceed with the APMR under the relevant conditions.
